"Over the moon" means to be extremely happy or delighted about something. Not just a little happy — very, deeply happy. Think of the biggest smile you've ever had on your face. That's the feeling this idiom describes.

The idiom comes from an old nursery rhyme you may have heard:

"Hey diddle diddle, the cat and the fiddle, the cow jumped over the moon..."

A cow jumping over the moon is, of course, impossible. But that's exactly the point — the image captures something so wonderful and extraordinary that it feels like anything is possible, even the unimaginable. Over time, the phrase "over the moon" was borrowed from this rhyme to describe a feeling of pure, sky-high joy.

The phrase has been in common use in English since at least the late 1800s, and it remains very popular today, especially in British English.

You use "over the moon" when someone receives unexpectedly wonderful news or when something makes them feel pure, uncomplicated joy.

It is almost always followed by "about" or "with" to tell us what caused the happiness:

  • "She was over the moon about her promotion."
  • "He was over the moon with joy when his daughter was born."

You can also use it without "about" or "with" when the reason is already clear from the context:

  • "Did you hear she got into her dream university? She's absolutely over the moon!"

These examples show how the idiom works naturally in everyday speech:

  • "I passed my driving test on the first attempt — I was over the moon!"
  • "The team scored in the final minute. Their coach was over the moon."
  • "She got a surprise birthday party and was absolutely over the moon about it."
  • "We finally adopted a puppy. The kids are over the moon."
  • "My grandmother was over the moon when she heard we were getting married."

Notice how in all these cases, the happiness is big, genuine, and heartfelt — not just mild pleasure.

This is important: "over the moon" is not used for small everyday happiness. You wouldn't say "I found a good parking spot and I'm over the moon." That would sound strange — even sarcastic.

It is reserved for truly significant moments, such as:

  • Getting a dream job or promotion
  • The birth of a child
  • Winning a competition
  • Receiving wonderful, unexpected news
  • A long-awaited achievement

Think of it as happiness that is so big, it has "launched" you right off the Earth and sent you flying over the moon.

"Over the moon" is an informal idiom. This means it fits perfectly in:

  • Everyday conversation with friends and family
  • Casual writing (text messages, social media, informal emails)
  • Interviews or speeches where you want to sound warm and human

It would feel too informal for:

  • Formal business writing or legal documents
  • Academic papers
  • Highly official announcements

However, it is worth noting that even public figures — politicians, sportspeople, celebrities — regularly use this phrase in interviews because it sounds warm, genuine, and relatable. So it sits on the border between casual and semi-formal speech comfortably.
Word You Can Pair With It

In natural speech, people often add words to strengthen the idiom. The most common ones are:

  • "absolutely" — "I'm absolutely over the moon."
  • "completely" — "She was completely over the moon."
  • "just" — "We're just over the moon about this."

These additions make the expression sound even more enthusiastic and heartfelt.

If you want to express the same idea in different words, here are some alternatives that mean roughly the same thing:

  • On cloud nine — extremely happy (very common in American English)
  • On top of the world — feeling wonderful, like nothing can go wrong
  • Thrilled — a simpler, one-word equivalent
  • Ecstatic — very formal; means intensely happy
  • Walking on air — so happy it feels like floating
  • In seventh heaven — in a state of perfect bliss

Of these, "over the moon" and "on cloud nine" are the two most popular idioms for extreme happiness in everyday English.

Don't use this idiom to describe someone else's happiness in a sarcastic or negative context — it will confuse people. "Over the moon" almost always carries a genuine, positive tone. It's not typically used ironically the way some phrases can be.

QuestionAnswer

What does it mean? Extremely, deeply happy about something.
When to use it? When celebrating big, joyful, meaningful moments.
Who uses it? Anyone speaking informal or conversational English, especially in Britain.
What follows it? Usually "about" or "with," then the reason for the joy.
How intense is it? Very — it's one of the strongest everyday phrases for happiness.

The next time you hear someone say "I'm over the moon!" — you'll know they aren't just pleased. They are beaming with joy, as if happiness itself has launched them right past the clouds and sent them soaring through the night sky.
